h1: Phoenix hops for chocolate and molasses notes in stout
title: Phoenix Hops for Chocolate in Stout | Craft Beer School
desc: Phoenix hops explained: an English dual purpose hop with chocolate, molasses and pine notes, how to use it in a homebrew stout and what to swap in.
teaser: A hop described as tasting of chocolate and molasses sounds like a joke. In a stout it makes sense.
standfirst: Phoenix is an English dual purpose hop with a spicy, resinous character that brewers often describe in terms of chocolate and molasses. That makes it an interesting choice for stouts and porters. Here is how to use it well at home.
sections:
Phoenix was bred at Wye in England and released in the mid 1990s. It was a seedling of Yeoman, an earlier English high alpha variety. It remains a niche English variety.

Alpha acid usually runs from about 8 to 13%, high enough for efficient bittering. The aroma is where Phoenix gets interesting. Descriptions include chocolate, molasses, pine and spice, with some floral notes.

Hops do not contain chocolate. Phoenix's oils include spicy, woody and resinous compounds that some tasters read as dark sweet notes. In a pale ale, most people would call it spicy and piney. In a stout, those notes sit next to roasted malt and the drinker's brain fills in chocolate and treacle.

That is the honest expectation. Phoenix will not make a stout taste like a chocolate bar. It adds a spicy, dark edge that fits the roast rather than fighting it. The chocolate in the glass still comes mostly from chocolate malt.

Here is a sweet-leaning stout at about OG 1.056 and 35 IBU:

  • Maris Otter pale malt 3.9 kg (75%).
  • Flaked oats 0.42 kg (8%).
  • Crystal malt around 150 EBC 0.31 kg (6%).
  • Chocolate malt 0.31 kg (6%).
  • Roasted barley 0.26 kg (5%).
  • Phoenix at 10% alpha, 60 minutes: about 26 g for 33 IBU.
  • Phoenix 20 g at 10 minutes for flavour.

Mash at 67 °C for body. Ferment with an English ale yeast at 18 to 19 °C. Skip the dry hop. In a stout, a little late Phoenix is enough.
The floor detail: watch the roast barley

At home, the easiest stout mistake is too much roasted barley. At 5% of the grist it gives a dry, coffee-like finish. At 10% or more it can turn acrid, especially with soft water. Phoenix adds its own spicy bitterness on top.

If your stout tastes harsh, cut the roasted barley before you cut the hops. Then taste again. A hop that is meant to add dark, spicy notes gets blamed for harshness that the grain bill caused.

Phoenix also suits:

  • Porters, where the same spicy dark notes work under brown and chocolate malt.
  • Strong bitters and old ales, as a bittering hop with a bit of character.
  • Winter ales with dark sugar or treacle, where molasses notes double up.

In pale beers it is less distinctive. The spice can feel muddy against crisp pale malt. For a pale ale, a fruitier hop such as Palisade or the classic Goldings will serve you better. Save Phoenix for the beers where dark malt gives its spice something to lean on. Because most of the flavour in a dark beer comes from the grain, a stout is also a forgiving place to try an unfamiliar hop without fussing over every late addition.

Phoenix is a niche crop. Indian homebrew suppliers rarely stock it as a standard item. You may need to ask for it or buy from an importer who brings in English hops to order. When you do get it, store it sealed in the freezer. The spicy, resinous oils fade with warmth and air.

If you cannot find Phoenix, Challenger gives a similar English bittering backbone with a spicier, more marmalade profile. Northdown adds cedar and pine. Neither has the exact dark note, but both work in a stout.
Taste the hop before the beer

A simple trick before you brew with an unfamiliar hop: steep a few pellets in hot water for a couple of minutes, let it cool and smell it. You can also rub a crushed pellet between your palms. It will not tell you exactly how the beer will taste, but it gives you a reference point. With Phoenix, you will smell the spice and resin straight away.

Write down what you smell. Then compare it with the finished stout. Building that habit is how brewers learn which hop notes survive into beer.
Why hop character changes in dark beer

The same hop can taste different in a pale ale and a stout. Roast malt lowers pH, adds its own bitterness and masks some hop aromas while amplifying others. Knowing how malt and hops interact is the part of recipe design that turns a good stout into one you can repeat.
faqs: Does Phoenix really taste of chocolate?
Not literally. Its spicy, resinous oils read as dark, chocolate and molasses-like notes next to roasted malt. The chocolate in a stout still comes mostly from the malt.
What is the alpha acid of Phoenix?
Phoenix usually tests between about 8 and 13% alpha acid, so it bitters efficiently.
Challenger or Northdown are the usual English swaps. Neither copies the dark note exactly, but both suit stouts and porters.
